links.note: 511 says the man to employ is one whose nature, having looked into good and bad (நன்மையும் தீமையும் நாடி), has taken to the good (நலம்புரிந்த தன்மையான்). 422 defines understanding as not letting the mind go wherever it goes but turning it from bad to good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது). The test for a king's officer is the book's general definition of அறிவு applied to a person at work.

504 tells the king to examine a man's qualities and faults and judge by what predominates (குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி ... மிகைநாடி). 511 uses the same verb நாடி, but now it is the candidate who examines good and bad and settles on the good. The king's weighing of the man in chapter 51 becomes, in chapter 52, a check on how the man himself weighs.

385 defines a king as one able to create sources, gather, guard and apportion (இயற்றலும் ஈட்டலும் காத்தலும் காத்த வகுத்தலும்). 512 wants the officer to enlarge the sources, build up the yield and look into what befalls them (வாரி பெருக்கி வளம்படுத்து உற்றவை ஆராய்வான்). The servant's qualification repeats the king's own economic duties one level down; Parimelazhagar's note on 512 points back to 385 for what the 'sources' are.

513 places trust in one who has love, understanding, clarity and freedom from desire (அன்பறிவு தேற்றம் அவாவின்மை). 682 opens with the same pair, அன்பறிவு, and adds considered eloquence as the three things an envoy cannot lack. The two lists share a core of loyalty and knowledge and then differ by office: the officer handling affairs needs steadiness and no greed, the envoy needs speech.

501 says a man is trusted after being examined through four things: virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life (அறம்பொருள் இன்பம் உயிரச்சம் நான்கின் திறந்தெரிந்து). 513 names four qualities the trusted man must firmly have (இந்நான்கும் நன்குடையான்). One four is the set of tests, the other the set of results; அவாவின்மை in 513 is what passing the wealth and pleasure tests of 501 would show.

510 says that doubting a man one has examined and trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு) brings endless trouble. 514 says that even when tested in every way (எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும்), many people turn different through the nature of the work (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும்). Read together, 514 limits 510: testing does not settle the matter, so the ban on doubt cannot mean a ban on watching how the man changes in office.

505 makes each person's own deeds the touchstone of greatness and smallness (தத்தம் கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்). 514 says tests of every kind before the appointment still leave many who change once in the work. Both put the decisive evidence in action, and 514 adds that the action that counts is the work itself, after trust has been given.

514 observes that many who passed every test turn different through the work (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும் மாந்தர் பலர்). 520 tells the king to look into the one doing the work every day (நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன்). The chapter's closing instruction answers the problem 514 raises: since office changes people, examination has to continue after appointment.

507 says that trusting those who lack knowledge, with fondness as the ground (காதன்மை கந்தா அறிவறியார்த் தேறுதல்), brings every folly. 515 says work is not to be assigned on the thought 'he is favoured' (சிறந்தானென்று ஏவற்பாற்றன்று) but only to one who knows, endures and can do it (அறிந்தாற்றிச் செய்கிற்பாற்கு). The same rule against affection as a credential is stated once for trust and once for assigning work; Parimelazhagar reads சிறந்தான் in 515 as 'one who loves us'.

515 requires for a task one who knows and endures and can carry it through (அறிந்தாற்றிச் செய்கிற்பாற்கு). 640 says that those without practical ability (திறப்பாடு இலாதவர்), though they plan in proper order, do things that never reach completion. 640 shows what 515's last requirement guards against: knowing is not enough without the capacity to finish.

516 asks the king to examine the doer, examine the deed, and act seeing how they fit the time (செய்வானை நாடி வினைநாடிக் காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்). 675 lists five things to think through before acting: resources, means, time, the deed and the place (பொருள்கருவி காலம் வினையிடனொடு ஐந்தும்). Deed and time are in both lists; 516 adds the one item 675 lacks, the person who will do it, which is the concern of a chapter on employing people.

516: examine the doer, the deed and the fit with the time, then act (காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்). 949: the trained physician acts after considering the measure of the patient, the measure of the illness and the time (உற்றான் அளவும் பிணியளவும் காலமும் ... கருதிச் செயல்). Both end in செயல் after a three-part assessment of person, matter and time, the same procedure in statecraft and in medicine.

517 says that once the king has reasoned 'this man will finish this by this means', he should leave it with him (அதனை அவன்கண் விடல்). 510 says that doubting one who has been examined and trusted brings endless trouble. Leaving the task with the man is the practical form of 510's rule: examination comes first and is then followed by a real handing over.

517 tells the king to leave the task to the chosen man (அவன்கண் விடல்). 520, in the same chapter, tells the king to look into the one doing the work daily (நாடோறும் நாடுக), because the world stays straight only if he does. The delegation in 517 is therefore not a withdrawal of attention; Parimelazhagar's note on 520 says the checking should be done privately so that the man's standing is not damaged.

509 says: trust no one without examining, and after examining, trust what is to be trusted (தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக தேறும் பொருள்). 518 has the same two steps for work: after establishing that a man is fit for the task (வினைக்குரிமை நாடிய பின்றை), make him the one it belongs to (அதற்குரியனாகச் செயல்). 518 carries 509 from inner trust to an outward grant; Parimelazhagar takes it as raising the man so he can finish the work on his own authority.

519 says fortune leaves the one who thinks otherwise of the closeness of a man devoted to the work (கேண்மை வேறாக நினைப்பானை நீங்கும் திரு). 808 praises those with the strength of intimacy not to listen to talk of a friend's lapse (கேளிழுக்கம் கேளாக் கெழுதகைமை). The duty not to reinterpret a close person's conduct appears in kingship and in friendship; Parimelazhagar reads 519 as the king being turned by the words of those who resent the officer, which is the situation 808 names.

519 warns the king against taking amiss the familiarity of a hard-working officer (வினைக்கண் வினையுடையான் கேண்மை). 700, addressed to the courtier, says that familiarity which does improper things on the thought 'we are old associates' (பழையம் எனக்கருதிப் பண்பல்ல செய்யும் கெழுதகைமை) brings ruin. The king must tolerate the liberty and the servant must not presume on it; each verse limits the other.

510 states that doubt about a man already examined and trusted brings endless trouble (தீரா இடும்பை). 519 gives a specific case and a specific cost: misreading the closeness of the man who is absorbed in the work drives away திரு, prosperity. The general warning of chapter 51 is here applied to the officer who has proved himself in office.

520: let the king look daily into the one doing his work (நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன்). 553: the king who does not look daily and do justice loses his land daily (நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன் நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்). The same phrase of daily examination is used for officers and for justice, and both tie the state of the land to that routine.

520 requires the king to examine the worker daily. 584 defines the spy as one who examines everyone, beginning with those who do the king's work (வினைசெய்வார்), then his kin and his enemies. 584 supplies the means by which the daily examination of 520 is carried out.

520 says that if the one doing the work does not bend, the world will not bend (கோடாமை கோடாது உலகு). 546 says victory comes from the king's sceptre, provided it does not bend (கோலதூஉங் கோடாதெனின்). கோடாமை, not bending, is the mark of the just sceptre, and 520 applies the same word to the officer, on whose straightness the world's straightness is made to depend.

521 says that honouring the old tie even when a man's means are gone (பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் பழைமை பாராட்டுதல்) is found among kin. 1047 says that one in poverty will be looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல நோக்கப்படும்). The conflict holds if 1047 is read as Pope reads it, of poverty in general; the verse's own qualifier அறஞ்சாரா, poverty unconnected with virtue, which Parimelazhagar and Subramuniyaswami keep, narrows it and reduces the conflict.

521: kin keep honouring old ties (பழைமை) even when all is lost. 806: those who keep within the bounds do not give up, even in ruin (தொலைவிடத்தும்), the bond of those who have stood with them from of old (தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் தொடர்பு). Loyalty to a long tie when fortune is gone is claimed as the mark of kin in one chapter and of true old friends in the other.

521 asserts that kin stand by a man when his means are gone. 796 says ruin has one benefit: it is a rod that measures one's கிளைஞர் at full length (கிளைஞரை நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல்). கிளைஞர் literally means kin, though Parimelazhagar takes it here as friends; on either reading 796 treats as something to be tested in adversity what 521 states as a fact about kin.

522 says that if a man gets kin whose love does not lapse (விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம் இயையின்), they give many gains (ஆக்கம் பலவும் தரும்). 884 says that if hidden enmity of unreformed mind appears, it gives many ills that turn his circle bad (இனமாணா ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்). The two verses have the same shape with opposite content, and Parimelazhagar notes that 'whose love does not lapse' in 522 is said to exclude the inner enmity of chapter 89: kin are an asset only on that condition.

523 compares the life of one who does not mingle freely to a tank's expanse filling with water without a bank (குளவளாக் கோடின்றி நீர்நிறைந்தற்று). 215 compares the wealth of a wise person who cares for the world to the village drinking tank filled with water (ஊருணி நீர்நிறைந்தற்று). Both end in the same words for wealth as a filled tank; in 215 the full tank serves the village, in 523 the water has nothing to hold it, which the commentators read as wealth that cannot be kept without kin.

524 says the fruit of having gained wealth is to live surrounded by one's kin (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட ஒழுகல்). 837 says that when a fool gets great wealth, strangers eat their fill and his own people go hungry (ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர்பசிப்பர்). 837 shows the failure of exactly the use 524 names: wealth that does not reach one's own people has missed its purpose.

524 names the purpose of gained wealth as living surrounded by kin (செல்வந்தான் பெற்றத்தால் பெற்ற பயன்). 212 says all wealth won by effort exists for doing good to the deserving (வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு). Both verses state what wealth is for and place it outside the owner; the Book of Virtue names the deserving in general, the chapter on a king's kin names the circle around him.

525 says one who can give and speak pleasantly (கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின்) will be surrounded by kin in layers. 387 says that for one able to give with pleasant words and protect (இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க வல்லார்க்கு), the world is as he sees it and follows his word. The same pair of means, gifts and kind speech, wins the circle of kin in one verse and the whole world in the other.

526 says no one on earth has a larger following than one who gives greatly and does not cherish anger (பெருங்கொடையான் பேணான் வெகுளி). 306 says anger, the fire that kills what it touches, burns the safe raft that is one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப்புணையைச் சுடும்). 306 gives the reason for the second condition in 526: anger destroys the circle that generosity gathers.

525 names giving and pleasant speech as what surrounds a man with kin. 526 keeps giving, now great giving (பெருங்கொடை), and replaces pleasant speech with not cherishing anger (பேணான் வெகுளி), and raises the result to a following unmatched on earth. The pair is not a repetition: the second verse moves from a positive manner to the removal of what drives people away.

527 says crows do not hide what they find but call the others and eat (காக்கை கரவா கரைந்துண்ணும்), and gain belongs only to people of that nature. 229 says that eating alone to fill up one's own store (தாமே தமியர் உணல்) is more bitter than begging. One verse commends shared eating through the crow and the other condemns eating alone; 527 adds the claim that sharing is also where prosperity lies.

527 ties gain (ஆக்கம்) to those who, like the crow, call others before eating. 227 says the disease of hunger does not touch one who is habituated to sharing his food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை). Both hold that sharing food protects the sharer's own fortune, stated in the Book of Virtue as freedom from hunger and here as prosperity.

527 praises the crow for not hiding (கரவா) its food and for calling others to eat. 1035 says those who live by eating what their own hands produce do not beg and give to those who ask without hiding (கரவாது). Not concealing what one has, கரவு being the book's word for the withholder's fault in chapters 106 and 107, is the shared mark of the crow and of the farmer.

528 says that if the king looks at people not in common but according to rank (பொதுநோக்கான் வேந்தன் வரிசையா நோக்கின்), many will live looking to that. 972 says birth is alike for all, but distinction is not alike, because of the difference in what people do (சிறப்பொவ்வா செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான்). 972 gives a basis for the differential regard of 528: Parimelazhagar reads வரிசை there as each person's merit, and 972 locates such difference in conduct, not birth.

528 tells the king not to look on everyone with a common eye but by rank. 541 defines justice as examining and acting without partiality toward anyone at all (கண்ணோடாது ... யார்மாட்டும்). The two fit only if their fields are kept apart: honour and attention are graded by merit, while judgment of wrongs is the same for all, so 541 marks the limit of 528.

528 ends: many will live looking to that (அதுநோக்கி வாழ்வார் பலர்). 542 says the world lives looking to the sky and the people live looking to the king's sceptre (கோல்நோக்கி வாழுங் குடி). The phrase 'live looking to' makes the king's conduct something people depend on as they depend on rain; 528 uses it for his recognition of each person's worth.

529 says those who were one's own and left will return to kinship when the cause of the discord is absent (அமராமைக் காரணம் இன்றி வரும்). 633 lists among a minister's abilities reuniting those who have parted (பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்). 529 says how that reunion comes about: the ground of the estrangement has to be removed, which Parimelazhagar takes as a fault on the king's own side.

529 says estranged kin return of themselves once the cause of discord is gone. 530 turns to one who left and has come back for a reason (காரணத்தின் வந்தானை) and tells the king to attend to it and accept him only after reflection (இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்). The pair separates two kinds of return, one that follows from the king's own correction and one prompted by the returner's interest, and prescribes welcome for the first and caution for the second.

530 says the king should attend to the reason for which a man who left has come back, wait, and accept him after thinking it over (இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்). 830 says that when an enemy turns friend, one should be friendly in face and withhold the heart (முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்). Both deal with someone who comes over after having been apart and both withhold immediate trust, but 530 ends in acceptance of the kinsman while 830 ends in letting the former enemy go.

509 gives the rule: trust no one without examining, then trust (தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது). 530 applies examination to a man who was already one's own, left, and came back for a reason: he is to be received after reflection (எண்ணிக் கொளல்). Leaving resets the earlier trust, so the test of chapter 51 has to be done again.
